explanations.explanation: This feature is a formatting‐marker detector: it lights up on the very first token inside a Markdown-style bold or heading span (e.g. the first word or number after “**”), signaling the start of an emphasized title, list item or section label.

This feature detects “meta-text” markers—tokens that introduce or delimit annotations and non-narrative bits (apostrophes in contractions, date/month tokens, comment-header symbols, license-block keywords, include-directives, etc.). It essentially flags structural‐or‐metadata boundaries rather than ordinary prose.

This neuron consistently fires on subword units that carry the core meaning of a content word (the root or stem morpheme), across languages—i.e. it flags the central lexical piece (“accompl-,” “particul-,” “inform-,” “fetal,” “pregun-,” “nou-,” “syst-,” “finn-/finns,” etc.) rather than affixes or purely function‐word fragments.

This neuron fires on expressions of ability or inability—tokens like “able,” “unable” and related negated auxiliaries (“don’t,” “isn’t,” “didn’t,” etc.) that mark statements about what can or can’t be done.
This neuron is a disjunction‐marker detector.  It lights up strongly on instances of “or” (and on slashes “/” when used to signal alternatives) – i.e. tokens that introduce a choice or alternative.
The feature is a marker for sentence‐ or title‐initial tokens—especially the first (often capitalized or numeric) word in paper titles or section headings—flagging the start of a new segment.

explanations.explanation: This neuron is a “segment‐boundary” detector.  It lights up on tokens that begin or end a logical unit—start‐of‐line words (e.g. “Friday”, “Over”), end‐of‐sentence punctuation, blank‐line separators in email threads, or the final keyword in C/C++ preprocessor directives (e.g. the last token of “#include…”, “#ifndef…”, “#pragma once”, etc.).

This feature fires on low-frequency, domain-specific jargon and proper nouns—i.e. the technical terms (medical-science, programming APIs, sports roles/contracts, legal/license phrases, etc.) that signal a specialized or academic-style text.
This feature fires on mentions of the FFmpeg multimedia‐transcoding tool—i.e. references to using “ffmpeg” (and its variants) in video/audio conversion or processing contexts.
This neuron is firing on the apostrophe in English negative contractions (e.g. the ’ in “don’t”), effectively marking lexical negation via the contraction.
